newsitem.title: FRANCE: French farmers silent on left's election win.
newsitem.headline: French farmers silent on left's election win.

text.p: French farmers, traditionally solid supporters of the right in the countryside, fell silent on Monday after the left swept their mentors from office amid fears of radical changes to European Union farm support.

Just as uncertainty about monetary union kept financial markets on edge as the Socialist Party headed for Sunday's upset victory, farmers had their eye on future farm talks designed to expand the EU eastwards.
Many fear subsidies will be capped in the drive to take in new member countries after the turn of the century, while others worry a new government would be less robust on farm exports.
Representatives from both major farm unions, the broad-based FNSEA and the powerful CNJA union of young farmers, declined to comment on the Socialist-led victory in parliamentary elections.
"We will wait and see what happens," CNJA head Christiane Lambert said -- words echoed almost exactly by the FNSEA.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac asked Socialist leader Lionel Jospin on Monday to form a government after his gamble in calling elections a year early blew up in his face and took his centre-right allies down to defeat.

Addressing the French Senate in April, Jospin said he was in favour of putting a ceiling on direct EU payments to farm producers in return for limiting production and for fairer distribution of subsidies among farmers.

That would seem mainly aimed at France's "grain baron" cereal farmers operating mostly north of the Loire, who receive advantages for setting aside idle cropland and have been accused by some smaller groups of hogging too many subsidies.
Fruit and dairy farmers have been particularly bitter about falling prices and staged a series of angry protests.

Grain farmers argue, however, that cereals make up a big slice of France's 100-billion-franc ($17 billion) annual export surplus and have become a vital source of food supply to the Third World as global stocks come under increasing pressure.
France is Europe's biggest agricultural producer and a major world grain exporter.
Jospin has not said who will fill the shoes of outgoing conservative farm minister Philippe Vasseur, a former journalist and free-trade sceptic who scored a hit with most farmers.
But grain markets were focusing nervously on reports in the past week that the job might go to a Communist minister likely to scale down support to larger, more efficient farms.
"People are a little nervous about all this," said one European grain trader.
Jospin, who needs the support of Communists to control parliament and may appoint one or more Communist ministers, said on Monday he would form a government in the next few days.
A Communist Party statement issued on Monday called for seats in government but did not mention individual ministries.

Farm unions said an EU summit in Amsterdam this month would be crucial to clarifying France's position on monetary union, but also that on the subsidised Common Agricultural Policy. Its critics led by Britain say the $50 billion regime must be cut to make way for EU enlargement.
Farmers would also like France's new government to honour a draft farm law spearheaded by Vasseur that was to have promoted French food exports on world markets and rural development.

Another key issue is likely to be the aftermath of last year's beef crisis caused by human health fears over mad cow disease or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). Unions will resist any rapid easing of an EU embargo on British beef export without pledges that consumer confidence will not slump again. ($1 = 5.8 francs)
